KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Plate — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the plate as the host’s tool: one plate per seat, handed out with ceremony, counted as they land — and the empty plate’s trip to the sink ends the job.

What is this?

A plate is the round cream plate with the green rim where dinner lands — and setting the table is the first hosting job a child can fully own.

What does it mean?

A named plate gives a child ownership of their own eating space — picky eaters often accept food on "their" plate that they reject off it. And counting plates per seat is early maths at dinner speed.

What does the child need to know?

You need the plates and the seat map: "one for daddy… one for grandma… one for YOU." The child sets; the family arrives. The sink delivery is the finish line.

Why this matters

A table set by the child makes the child part of the meal before the food lands — membership changes eating behaviour more than any bribe.

What it teaches

One-to-one matching (plate to seat), counting with purpose, carrying-with-two-hands care, and the host identity that sets tables for life.

Words to learn

plateset the tableseatcountemptysink

Say this to your child

“"Plate! One for daddy… one for grandma… one for YOU! Count the seats — everyone has a plate. The table is SET. And after dinner: empty plates to the sink, two hands, job done. What a host!"”

Step by step

  1. The job briefing: "plates! Tonight YOU set the table."
  2. The map: "how many seats? Count them… four! How many plates? Four — one each!"
  3. The handout, with ceremony: "daddy’s plate… grandma’s plate… YOUR plate." Each landing named.
  4. The gap check: "did everyone get one? A seat with no plate? Fix it, host!"
  5. The finish: after dinner, "empty plates to the sink — carry with two hands!" The job closes; the host bows.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "plate" sits over a cream plate with a green rim — round, ready and waiting for dinner’s landing.

Ask your child

"How many seats tonight?" "Whose plate is this?" "Where do empty plates go?" (the sink!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might count the family nightly, correct a missing plate, or refuse to eat off any plate but "mine" — the host, seated at their own table.

Out in the real world

Plates stack in every cupboard and queue at every buffet. "One per seat" scales to picnics, parties and restaurants — the host’s rule is universal.

Try it together

Restaurant Night: menus, orders (real food), and the child sets every place before cooking starts. The tip is a thank-you; the repeat customers are guaranteed.

Understanding check

Ask: "What lands on the plate?" (dinner!) "How many plates per seat?" (one) "What do we do after?" (sink — two hands!)

This lesson pairs with the Plate flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.
